/NTgCalls/Build Guide.xml:
Introduction

Being a modern library, NTgCalls requires CMake 3.27+ and Python 3.10+ to be built on your system. On Linux it also needs libasound2 and libpulse-dev. We recommend using the latest version of CMake. Before building NTgCalls, check for pre-compiled shared libs on GitHub Releases, Python bindings on PyPI, the Node.js package on npm or the crate on crates.io. Building from source may be necessary if pre-compiled packages are not available. On Linux x86_64, macOS and Android the build downloads its own Clang toolchain, so there is nothing to install by hand. Linux ARM64 is the only platform that uses the system compiler.

Installing Prerequisites

Below, we will guide you through the step-by-step process of installing the prerequisites required to compile NTgCalls on your operating system.

Linux

Update the system's package list:
First, make sure you have an updated list of packages: $ sudo apt update Install the build dependencies:
On ARM64 the toolchain is not downloaded, so Clang has to come from the system: x86_64 ARM64 $ sudo apt install libx11-dev build-essential curl libasound2-dev libpulse-dev $ sudo apt install libx11-dev build-essential curl libasound2-dev libpulse-dev $ curl -s https://apt.llvm.org/llvm.sh | sudo bash -s -- 22

Windows

Install Microsoft Visual Studio 2022:
Install Microsoft Visual Studio 2022 with the C++ workload. You can download it from the official website. Download CMake Installer:
Download the CMake installer for Windows from the official website. Run Installer:
Run the downloaded CMake installer and follow the installation wizard instructions. Make sure to select the option to add CMake to the system PATH during installation.

macOS

Install Xcode Command Line Tools:
If you don't have Xcode installed, you can install the Command Line Tools separately. Open a terminal and run the following command: $ xcode-select --install Install CMake:
Open a terminal and run the following command to install CMake: $ brew install cmake

Cloning and Building

In this section, you'll learn how to clone the NTgCalls repository and build the library from source.

Cloning the Repo

To begin building NTgCalls from source, you need to clone the GitHub repository. Follow these steps to clone the repo: Change to the Directory Where You Want to Clone the Repo:
Navigate to the directory where you want to store the NTgCalls source code. You can use the cd command to change directories. $ cd /path/to/your/directory Clone the NTgCalls Repository:
Use the following command to clone the NTgCalls GitHub repository: $ git clone https://github.com/pytgcalls/ntgcalls.git --recursive

Compilation

Every binding is built through the same entry point, setup.py build_lib, which takes the target you want and reads how to build it from that target's own configuration. Run every command from the root directory of the project. It's essential to have Python 3.10+ installed on your system.

Shared Library

For developers looking to use NTgCalls with C and C++, we provide C bindings. This is the default target, so it needs no --target: Shared Static $ python3 setup.py build_lib $ python3 setup.py build_lib --static The libraries and the generated ntgcalls.h are written to shared-output or static-output.

Python Bindings

The Python bindings are installed like any other package, and the extension is compiled as part of the install: $ pip3 install . -U

Node.js Bindings

The Node.js addon is built through the same command, and lands in targets/node/build/Release: $ python3 setup.py build_lib --target=node

Rust Crate

The crate links against the C shared library. Build it once, then point the crate at the result through NTGCALLS_LIB_DIR, otherwise the build script downloads the matching release from GitHub: $ python3 setup.py build_lib --static $ NTGCALLS_LIB_DIR=$PWD/static-output/lib cargo build --manifest-path targets/rust/Cargo.toml

Java for Android Bindings

The Android target builds the native libraries for all four ABIs, then Gradle packs them into the archive: Generate the .so libraries for the Android platform: $ python3 setup.py build_lib --target=android Build the Android project: $ cd targets/android $ ./gradlew build assembleRelease Get the .aar file:
Copy the generated .aar file to your desired directory: $ cp app/build/outputs/aar/app-release.aar /path/to/your/directory

Other Options

build_lib also accepts --no-preserve-cache to drop the build directory once it is done, and --defines=key=value;key2=value2 to override any substitution the target configuration uses. Two more commands are available: list_targets prints the targets that can be built, and generate writes the language-agnostic schema every binding and the documentation are generated from, without building anything. $ python3 setup.py list_targets $ python3 setup.py generate

/NTgCalls/Client.xml:
Client

The NTgCalls Client is your primary interface for interacting with Telegram Calls. This page covers what surrounds the API: how to create and dispose of an instance, how to read the library version, and how to route the library logs into your own logging setup. Everything else is documented in the Reference section.

Example

Python C Node.js Java Rust import ntgcalls app = ntgcalls.NTgCalls() print(app.ping()) #include "ntgcalls.h" int main() { ntg_instance* handle = ntg_instance_create(); char* out = NULL; ntg_ping(&out); ntg_instance_destroy(handle); return 0; } const { NTgCalls } = require('ntgcalls'); const app = new NTgCalls(); console.log(await NTgCalls.ping()); import io.github.pytgcalls.NTgCalls; NTgCalls app = new NTgCalls(); System.out.println(NTgCalls.ping()); use ntgcalls::NTgCalls; let app = NTgCalls::new(); println!("{}", NTgCalls::ping()?);

Lifecycle

class ntgcalls.NTgCalls() The instance owns every connection you open through it. It is released by the garbage collector, and every call it still holds is stopped at interpreter exit, so there is nothing to dispose of by hand.
LIBRARY VERSION ntgcalls.__version__: str Version of the native library the bindings were built against. ntg_instance* ntg_instance_create() Creates an instance and returns the handle every other function takes as its first argument. The handle is yours to release.

LIBRARY VERSION const char* ntg_get_version() Version of the native library. The returned string is owned by the library.
ERROR DETAIL const char* ntg_last_error() Message of the last failure on the calling thread. Every function returns an ntg_result code, and this is where the detail behind it lives. class NTgCalls() The instance owns every connection you open through it and is released by the garbage collector, so there is nothing to dispose of by hand. class NTgCalls() The constructor loads the native library and allocates the instance. The native side is released when the object is finalized, so there is nothing to dispose of by hand. Logging

The library reports its own diagnostics and the ones coming from WebRTC. How they reach you depends on the binding. The logs are routed into the standard logging module, under the ntgcalls and webrtc loggers. Both are set to CRITICAL on import unless your application has already given them a level, so claim them before creating the instance to see anything. import logging logging.getLogger('ntgcalls').setLevel(logging.DEBUG) logging.getLogger('webrtc').setLevel(logging.WARNING) Install a callback to receive every message, along with its level, source, file and line. Passing NULL stops the delivery. void on_log(ntg_log_message message, void* user_data) { printf("%s:%u %s\n", message.file, message.line, message.message); } int main() { ntg_set_log_callback(&on_log, NULL); ... } The logs go to the console. Pick how much of them you want with setLogLevel, which accepts a value of the LogLevel enum. const { setLogLevel, LogLevel } = require('ntgcalls'); setLogLevel(LogLevel.WARNING); The logs go to the Android system log, under the ntgcalls tag. The logs are forwarded to the log crate, on the ntgcalls and ntgcalls::webrtc targets, so any logger implementation picks them up. use ntgcalls::log; log::init_logging();

Callbacks

Every callback is registered on the instance and documented, one page each, in the Callbacks section of the Reference.

Idle

This function will run indefinitely in order to block the main script execution and prevent it from exiting while having client(s) that are still running in the background. PyTgCalls works by keeping your handlers in a pool of worker threads, which run concurrently outside the main thread. Calling idle() will ensure that the client(s) remain active, by preventing the main script from ending until you decide to quit. Once a signal is received (e.g.: from CTRL+C) the function will terminate and your main script will continue.

Example

from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls from pytgcalls import idle ... app1 = PyTgCalls(client1) app2 = PyTgCalls(client2) app3 = PyTgCalls(client3) ... # Set handlers up app1.start() app2.start() app3.start() idle()

/PyTgCalls/Calling Methods.xml:
Calling Methods

At this point, we have successfully installed PyTgCalls and installed an MTProto client; we are now aiming towards the core of the library. It’s time to start playing with the API!

Basic Usage

Making API method calls with PyTgCalls is very simple. Here’s a basic example we are going to examine step by step: from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls from pytgcalls import idle ... api_id = 12345 api_hash = '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef' ... app = PyTgCalls(client) app.start() app.play( -1001185324811, 'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4', ) idle()

Basic step-by-step

Let’s begin by importing the Client class and idle function: from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls from pytgcalls import idle Now let’s import your MTProto Client: PyrogramMod Telethon Hydrogram from pyrogram import Client from telethon import TelegramClient from hydrogram import Client Set your api_id and api_hash taken from my.telegram.org: api_id = 12345 api_hash = '0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef' Initialize the MTProto client: PyrogramMod Telethon Hydrogram client = Client('test_session', api_id, api_hash) client = TelegramClient('test_session', api_id, api_hash) client = Client('test_session', api_id, api_hash) Initialize the PyTgCalls client: app = PyTgCalls(client) Start the PyTgCalls client: app.start() Now you can call any method you want: app.play( -1001185324811, 'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4', ) Lastly, call the idle function to keep your code running: idle()

Asynchronous Calls

In case you wish to run PyTgCalls asynchronously: import asyncio from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls from pytgcalls import idle ... app = PyTgCalls(client) async def main(): await app.start() await app.play( -1001185324811, 'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4', ) await idle() asyncio.run(main())

Asynchronous step-by-step

Import PyTgCalls, AsyncIO and create an instance: import asyncio from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls from pytgcalls import idle ... app = PyTgCalls(client) Async methods can’t be executed at the top level, because they must be within an async-defined function; here, we define one, and we put our code inside it; method calls require the await keyword: async def main(): await app.start() await app.play( -1001185324811, 'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4', ) await idle() Then, we tell asyncio to call main() in async mode asyncio.get_event_loop().run_until_complete(main())

Filters

Filters are objects that can be used to filter the content of incoming updates. Read more about how filters work.

Details

pytgcalls.filters.create() Easily create a custom filter. Custom filters give you extra control over which updates are allowed or not to be processed by your handlers.
PARAMETERS func: callable A function that accepts three positional arguments (filter, client, update) and returns a boolean: True if the update should be handled, False otherwise. The filter argument refers to the filter itself and can be used to access keyword arguments (read below). The client argument refers to the Client that received the update. The update argument type will vary depending on which Handler is coming from. Your function body can then access the incoming update attributes and decide whether to allow it or not. name: Optional[str] Your filter’s name. Can be anything you like. Defaults to "CustomFilter". **kwargs: Optional[Any] Any additional keyword arguments you want to pass to your filter function.
pytgcalls.filters.me Filter updates for yourself.
pytgcalls.filters.stream_end() Filter updates for when a stream ends. PARAMETERS stream_type: Optional[StreamEnded.Type] Pass one or more stream type to filter stream end updates. device: Optional[Device] Pass one or more devices to filter stream end updates.
pytgcalls.filters.chat() Filter updates coming from one or more chats. You can use set bound methods to manipulate the chats container.
PARAMETERS chats: Union[int, str, list] Pass one or more chat ids/usernames to filter chats. Defaults to None (no chats).
pytgcalls.filters.chat_update() Filter specific type of chat updates.
PARAMETERS flags: ChatUpdate.Status Pass one or more flags to filter chat updates. pytgcalls.filters.call_participant() Filter updates for when a call participant joins, leaves or is updated.
PARAMETERS flags: Optional[GroupCallParticipant.Action] Pass one or more flags to filter call participant updates. pytgcalls.filters.stream_frame() Filter updates for when stream frames are received.

Handling Updates

Calling API methods sequentially is cool, but what if, for example, the list of participants changes? This page covers updates and how to handle such events in PyTgCalls. Let’s have a look at how they work.

Defining Updates

First of all, let's define what these updates are. As hinted earlier, updates are events that happen in PyTgCalls, such as joining a group call, changes in the participant list, stream ended etc. They are meant to notify you about a new specific state change. These updates are handled by registering one or more callback functions in your app using Decorators. Each handler deals with a specific event. When a matching update arrives from Telegram or NTgCalls, the registered callback function will be called back by the framework, and its body will execute.

Registering a Handler

To explain how handlers work, let's examine the one that will be in charge of handling StreamVideoEnded updates, which occur when a video stream ends. The same setup logic is shared with every type of handler, and you should not have troubles settings them up once you have learned from this section. You can mix def and async def handlers as much as you need, PyTgCalls will still work concurrently and efficiently regardless of what you choose.

Using Decorators

The most elegant way to register a stream end handler is by using the on_stream_end() decorator: from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls, filters from pytgcalls.types import Update from pytgcalls.types import MediaStream ... app = PyTgCalls(client) @app.on_update(filters.stream_end()) async def my_handler(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update): if isinstance(update, StreamVideoEnded): await pytgcalls.play( -1001185324811, 'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4', ) app.run() The defined my_handler function, which accepts two arguments (client, update), will be executed whenever a new update arrives.

Using add_handler()

The add_handler() method takes any handler instance that wraps around your defined callback function and registers it in your Client. It is useful in case you want to programmatically add handlers. from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls, filters from pytgcalls.types import Update from pytgcalls.types import MediaStream ... app = PyTgCalls(client) async def my_handler(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update): if isinstance(update, StreamVideoEnded): await pytgcalls.play( -1001185324811, 'http://docs.evostream.com/sample_content/assets/sintel1m720p.mp4', ) app.add_handler(my_handler, filters.stream_end()) app.run()
/PyTgCalls/Install Guide.xml:
Install Guide

Being a modern Python library, PyTgCalls requires Python 3.10+ to be installed in your system. We recommend using the latest versions of both Python 3 and pip. Get Python 3 from the Python website or use your package manager. Get pip by following the instructions here. PyTgCalls only supports Python 3, starting from version 3.10.

Install PyTgCalls

The easiest way to install and upgrade PyTgCalls to its latest stable version is by using pip: $ pip3 install -U py-tgcalls

Bleeding Edge

PyTgCalls is always evolving: although new releases on PyPI are only published when a significant number of changes are added, this doesn’t mean you can’t try new features right now! In case you’d like to try out the latest PyTgCalls’ features, the GitHub repo is constantly updated with new changes; you can install the development version straight from the master branch using this command (note “master.zip” in the link): $ pip3 install -U git+https://github.com/pytgcalls/pytgcalls

Verifying

To verify that PyTgCalls is correctly installed, open a Python shell and import it. If no errors show up you are good to go. >>> import pytgcalls >>> pytgcalls.__version__ ''

Using Filters

So far we’ve seen how to register a decorator function that executes every time an update comes from the server, but there’s much more than that to come. Here we’ll discuss filters. Filters enable a fine-grain control over what kind of updates are allowed or not to be passed in your callback functions, based on their inner details.

Single Filters

Let’s start right away with a simple example: This example will show you how to only handle updates that are an Incoming Call and ignore any other update. Filters are passed as the first argument of the decorator: from pytgcalls import filters from pytgcalls.types import ChatUpdate ... @app.on_update(filters.chat_update(ChatUpdate.Status.INCOMING_CALL)) def on_incoming_call(client, update): print("Incoming call!", update) or, without decorators. Here filters are passed as the second argument of the add_handler function; the first is the callback function itself: from pytgcalls import filters from pytgcalls.types import ChatUpdate ... def on_incoming_call(client, update): print("Incoming call!", update) pytgcalls.add_handler(on_incoming_call, filters.chat_update(ChatUpdate.Status.INCOMING_CALL))

Combining Filters

Filters can be used in a more advanced way by inverting and combining more filters together using bitwise operators ~, & and |: Use ~ to invert a filter (behaves like the not operator). Use & and | to combine filters together (behaves like the and and or operators). Here are some examples: This example will show you how to only handle updates that are left updates from a specific chat and ignore any other update: from pytgcalls import filters from pytgcalls.types import ChatUpdate ... @app.on_update(~filters.chat_update(ChatUpdate.Status.LEFT_GROUP) & filters.chat(1234567890)) def on_incoming_voice_call(client, update): print("Left chat!", update) This example will show you how to only handle updates that are left updates or incoming call updates and from a specific chat: from pytgcalls import filters from pytgcalls.types import ChatUpdate ... @app.on_update(filters.chat(1234567890) & (filters.chat_update(ChatUpdate.Status.LEFT_GROUP) | filters.chat_update(ChatUpdate.Status.INCOMING_CALL))) def on_incoming_voice_call(client, update): print("Incoming voice call or left chat!", update)

Using Handlers

Handlers are used to instruct PyTgCalls to execute a specific function when a certain event occurs. For a much more convenient way to handle updates, you can use the decorators instead.

Registering Handlers

To register a handler, you need to use the add_handler method. This method takes two arguments: the first is the callback function, and the second is the filter. from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls from pytgcalls.types import Update from pytgcalls import filters as call_filters ... client = # Here Your MTProto Client app = PyTgCalls(client) async def handler(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update): print(update) ... app.add_handler(handler, call_filters.stream_end()) ...

Removing Handlers

To remove a handler, you need to use the remove_handler method. This method takes the callback function as its only argument. from pytgcalls import PyTgCalls from pytgcalls.types import Update ... client = # Here Your MTProto Client app = PyTgCalls(client) async def handler(client: PyTgCalls, update: Update): print(update) ... app.remove_handler(handler) ...
